# Loan Instrument Repair and Recall Checklist

Fictional Cedar Lantern Dance Studio. Training fixture only; no real studio policy.

## Opening a repair record
A repair report identifies the asset number and describes what happened in ordinary language. Students need not name a component correctly. Staff distinguish an observed defect from a guess about its cause, then mark whether the instrument can remain in use. Photographs can help locate a mark, but a photograph alone does not establish that a student caused it. The repair bench is not a place for public arguments about responsibility.

A borrower must report a split drumhead or loose metal fitting within 24 hours of discovering it. Stop playing and keep the instrument in its case while waiting for instructions. A report can be lodged even when the desk is closed; record when the issue was noticed and when the message was sent. Do not attempt a test strike to make a crack easier to hear.

## Return of a recalled instrument
A safety-recalled instrument must be returned by the end of the next business day, overriding its ordinary loan due date. The repair desk arranges a safe handover if the borrower cannot attend during opening hours. A recall message states the asset number, reason and collection contact. Returning another drum of the same colour does not satisfy the recall. The store's normal seven-day renewal does not extend this deadline.

When a safety recall interrupts a current loan, the repair desk offers a practice pad for the remaining original loan period at no additional deposit. This offer does not promise an identical drum. The borrower may decline the pad and still return the recalled asset on time. The pad receives its own checkout entry, but it is linked to the original receipt so that the desk does not accidentally charge another deposit.

## The deposit printed at the repair bench
The repair checklist requires a 30 dollar refundable deposit for a hand-drum kit. The store procedure gives a different current amount for that same standard kit. The repair desk has not announced that its checklist overrides the store procedure. Present the conflict rather than silently treating a repair form as the latest financial authority. A quote for replacing a head is a separate document and cannot answer which refundable loan deposit applies.

## Hygiene and consumables
Practice-pad surfaces are cleaned with the supplied dry microfiber cloth after each use; students must not spray them with disinfectant. Bench staff use a separate manufacturer-approved process between borrowers. A sticky surface is reported rather than scrubbed with an abrasive sponge. Consumable tape used by a teacher to mark a rhythm pattern belongs on the practice mat, not on the borrowed instrument or its case label.

The repair record tracks replaced components and the person who performed the inspection. A drum can look unchanged after an internal fitting has been secured. Staff therefore check the inspection tag rather than inferring safety from appearance. A student is welcome to ask what was done, but cannot sign a workshop release on behalf of the repair technician.

## Charges and disputed damage
The technician describes the repair and submits any proposed charge to administration. The checklist does not establish a fixed penalty for every mark, a depreciation rate, or an automatic liability rule. Staff must not invent such values from a deposit amount. The borrower can attach a written account and collection photograph to the record. Keep those materials private and do not circulate them through the class group chat.

## Returning equipment safely
A recalled kit waits behind the desk in the labelled isolation area. It must not be placed back into the open loan rack merely because another student needs it urgently. Staff arrange another practice activity rather than lending an uninspected item. If a case latch also fails, the clerk notes the latch issue separately and secures the lid for transport without using glue on the original case.

## Worked recall example
A student with a 21-day loan discovers a loose ring on day four and reports it that evening. The repair desk sends a safety recall the next morning. The student must follow the next-business-day deadline even though many ordinary loan days remain. A practice pad can cover the remaining original period without a second deposit. If the class teacher later asks for a renewal, the repaired drum still cannot leave isolation without the technician's inspection sign-off. The deposit disagreement between the two current documents remains a separate unresolved question.

## Distinguishing a repair from a loan
An inspection tag records the state of an asset after workshop checks; a loan receipt records who has the asset and for how long. Neither document replaces the other. An instrument can pass inspection and still be unavailable because it is reserved for another student. Equally, a borrower with a current receipt must stop using an instrument after a safety recall. Staff should explain which record answers the question being asked instead of using a reassuring green tag to dismiss a reported defect.

## Bench queue and communication
Repair requests are logged in received order, with safety concerns flagged for the technician. The checklist does not publish a promised repair completion time for every fault. A clerk may tell a borrower that an inspection is pending, but should not promise a next-day repair based only on an empty bench. Record the contact route requested by the family and send a clear update when the technician has a decision. A child should not be asked to negotiate a repair bill at the desk in front of classmates.
